summary: Presents four YANG 1.1 modules, three IETF ones (ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client, ietf-tls-server) and one supporting IANA module. The client and server modules support configuring and monitoring TLS endpoints, and the groupings are meant to be reused by models for protocols that run over TLS.

plainLanguage.summary:
Several management models need to configure a TLS client or a TLS server. Without a shared vocabulary, each of them invents its own way to describe the identity a device presents, the certificates it trusts, the TLS versions it allows and the cipher suites it will negotiate.

RFC 9645 supplies that vocabulary as reusable YANG groupings. Another model imports the grouping it needs and gets the same structure and the same names, without having to write TLS configuration from scratch.

subtitle: Reusable YANG building blocks for configuring the TLS client and TLS server inside any management data model.

tldr.problem: Many management models need to configure a TLS client or server, and each would otherwise define its own way to describe identities, trusted peers, TLS versions and cipher suites.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9645 defines three IETF YANG modules (ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client, ietf-tls-server) with groupings that other models import, plus a script IANA used to build an iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs module from its TLS Cipher Suites registry.
tldr.outcome: Models for HTTPS and for NETCONF over TLS can share one definition of TLS settings. The groupings cover only TLS itself, so ports and addresses come from a transport-level module such as RFC 9643.

today: RFC 9645 was published in October 2024 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Provides
sections.content:
This document presents four YANG 1.1 modules: three IETF modules and one IANA module. The three IETF modules are ietf-tls-common, ietf-tls-client and ietf-tls-server. The client and server modules are the primary products of the work, supporting the configuration and monitoring of TLS clients and servers.

The groupings are expected to be used together with the groupings of an underlying transport-level module, such as those in RFC 9643. The transport-level model is what carries the remote address, the remote port, the local address and the local port.

The IANA module is iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs, which defines YANG enumerations that mirror an IANA-maintained algorithm registry. IANA used the script in the RFC's appendix to generate it; the document does not publish the initial version, which IANA publishes and maintains.

The RFC says the three IETF modules model generic TLS clients and servers, where generic means the least common denominator rather than complete. Basic TLS support is provided and advanced features are left to augmentations by consuming modules. The groupings are meant for applications that need to configure TLS protocol stacks, such as the data models for HTTPS and for NETCONF over TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives other management models a ready-made way to describe a TLS client or a TLS server. It covers the common ground only, so each model can add whatever extra settings it needs.

sections.title: Where These Modules Fit
sections.content:
These four modules are part of a collection of RFCs that together support configuring both the clients and servers of NETCONF and RESTCONF. The crypto-types module has no dependencies of its own; the truststore module and the keystore module both depend on it; the transport-level modules for TCP, SSH and TLS sit above those; and the HTTP, NETCONF and RESTCONF client and server models sit above those in turn.

The ietf-tls-client and ietf-tls-server modules each define exactly one grouping, focused on TLS-specific configuration, and they deliberately avoid any transport-level configuration such as which ports to listen on or connect to. That leaves each application free to decide how the underlying TCP connection is established. The RFC gives an example: an application supporting NETCONF Call Home could use the server grouping for the TLS part and add its own nodes for the TCP-level call-home configuration.

Both TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 may be configured. TLS 1.2 is obsoleted by TLS 1.3 but is still in common use, so its feature statement is marked with the status deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: The TLS groupings deliberately say nothing about ports or addresses, so a model for, say, a call-home connection can decide those for itself. The RFC also keeps TLS 1.2 available for older peers, but marks that support as deprecated.

sections.title: Common TLS Settings
sections.content:
The common module holds what a TLS client and a TLS server both need. Its features are tls12, tls13, hello-params, asymmetric-key-pair-generation and supported-algorithms. It defines two base identities, one for TLS versions, from which tls12 and tls13 derive.

The hello-params-grouping configures the list of TLS algorithms the client or server will permit. The lists are ordered: if several algorithms are permitted by the client, the one that appears first in the client's list and is also permitted by the server is the one used for the connection. Being able to restrict the permitted algorithms lets a client or server comply with a local security policy. The grouping holds a tls-versions container with an optional minimum and maximum version, and a cipher-suites list, which is ordered by the user. To support both TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, the cipher suites part should carry three parameters: TLS Cipher Suites, TLS SignatureScheme and TLS Supported Groups.

The module also has two protocol-accessible nodes. A read-only supported-algorithms container reports the TLS algorithms the server supports. And an RPC called generate-asymmetric-key-pair generates a key pair, taking the algorithm, an optional number of bits and the encoding for the private key, which may be cleartext, encrypted by another key or hidden; the output is either the key pair or the location of a hidden key.
sections.plainLanguage: The common part holds the TLS versions and the cipher suites a client or server will accept. The cipher suite list is ordered, so the first entry both sides allow is the one used. The module can also report which algorithms a server supports and generate a key pair on request.

sections.title: The Client Grouping
sections.content:
The tls-client-grouping has four parts. client-identity configures the credentials the client presents, and it is optional because client authentication may happen at a higher protocol layer. It is a choice with four options, each enabled by a feature: a certificate, a raw public key with its private key, a TLS 1.2 pre-shared key, or a TLS 1.3 external pre-shared key. The certificate and key options reuse the keystore groupings, so the secret can be given inline or referred to in the central keystore. The TLS 1.3 external pre-shared key option also carries an external identity, an optional hash, and optional context, target protocol and target key derivation values.

server-authentication configures the trust anchors used to authenticate the server, again as a choice of options: CA certificates, end-entity certificates, raw public keys, TLS 1.2 pre-shared keys and TLS 1.3 external pre-shared keys. These reuse the truststore groupings.

hello-params brings in the common grouping described above. keepalives configures a presence container that tests whether the server is still alive at the TLS protocol layer, with an optional maximum wait and a maximum number of attempts, and an optional flag for whether the peer may send them.

The module defines only groupings. It has no protocol-accessible nodes of its own when implemented, because other modules instantiate the grouping where they need it.
sections.plainLanguage: The client grouping covers four things: the identity the client presents, the material it trusts to authenticate the server, the versions and cipher suites it will negotiate, and an optional liveness test of the server. The secrets can be given inline or referred to the device's keystore.

sections.title: The Server Grouping
sections.content:
The tls-server-grouping mirrors the client grouping. server-identity configures the credentials the server presents, as a choice of a certificate, a raw private key, a TLS 1.2 pre-shared key or a TLS 1.3 external pre-shared key, each enabled by a feature and reusing the keystore groupings. The TLS 1.2 pre-shared key option carries an optional identity hint.

client-authentication configures the trust anchors for authenticating the client. It is optional, because client authentication may happen at a higher protocol layer, and it offers the same choices as the client's server-authentication node. hello-params again brings in the common grouping.

keepalives configures a flag that lets the TLS client test whether the server is alive, plus a presence container that tests whether the client is alive, both at the TLS protocol layer. As with the client module, this module defines only groupings and no protocol-accessible nodes of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The server grouping is the mirror image of the client's: the identity the server presents, the material it trusts to authenticate clients, the versions and cipher suites it will negotiate, and optional liveness tests in both directions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The three IETF modules define groupings and will not be deployed as standalone modules, so their security implications depend on how they are used. The designers of modules that import them must do their own analysis.

The enumerations in the IANA module are not security sensitive, because they are statically defined in a publicly accessible module. IANA may deprecate or obsolete them over time as issues are found in the algorithms. The module defines no writable nodes, RPCs, actions or notifications.

In the common module, none of the readable or writable data nodes are considered sensitive, and no access control extensions are set. The one exception worth noting is the generate-asymmetric-key-pair RPC, which may, if the cleartext private keys feature is enabled and the client asks for it, return the private key in cleartext. The RFC says it is NOT RECOMMENDED for private keys to pass the server's security perimeter.

Every writable data node in the client module may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some environments, because any modification to a key or a reference to a key may dramatically change the security policy in force. The default-deny-write access control extension is therefore set on all of them. The server module is treated the same way. The RFC also points out that these modules use groupings from other modules that may define sensitive nodes, so the security considerations of those modules apply as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Because these are building blocks rather than finished models, the module that uses them has to do the security analysis. The one point the RFC singles out is that a key pair can be generated with the private key in cleartext, which is not recommended.

sections.title: The IANA Cipher Suite Module
sections.content:
IANA used the script in the RFC's appendix to generate the iana-tls-cipher-suite-algs YANG module, which is available from the "YANG Parameters" registry. IANA has added a note to the registry saying that new values must not be added to the module directly; they must instead be added to the "TLS Cipher Suites" registry in the "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Parameters" registry group.

When a value is added to that registry, a new enum statement must be added to the module. The statement replicates the name from the registry, carries the decimal value, includes a status only if the registration has been deprecated or obsoleted, has a description of the form "Enumeration for the 'TLS_FOO' algorithm", and replicates the references. Unassigned or reserved values do not appear in the module. An IANA recommendation of "N" maps to the YANG status deprecated.

When the module is updated, a new revision statement with a unique revision date is added in front of the existing ones, with a description saying why the update occurred and a reference pointing at the document that changed the registry. IANA has also added a note to the "TLS Cipher Suites" registry saying that the YANG module must be updated as defined in RFC 9645 whenever the registry changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher suite list is kept in step with IANA's registry by a generated module. The RFC tells IANA how to update it: add one enumeration per new registry entry, and record the change in a new revision of the module.
